Ukraine Needs Reformers, Not Populists In brief: As Ukraine enters the fifth year of full-scale war, a new political current is emerging. Sovereignism may appeal to wartime emotions – but it risks empowering populism over reform. By Michał Kujawski Aug. 9, 2026, 4:11 pm Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine. (Photo by Depositphotos) Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip In the fifth year of Russia’s full-scale invasion, the rhetoric of some Ukrainian politicians and public commentators suggests the emergence of a new political trend that could be described as sovereignism. This tendency is a direct product of political developments, the realities of the battlefield, and broader social change. It is, above all, a way of channeling the emotions generated by war. Since 2022, Ukrainians have demonstrated an extraordinary ability to adapt to extreme circumstances. They have displayed remarkable creativity, unconventional thinking, determination, courage and resilience. Their resistance has been nothing short of extraordinary. Yet these admirable qualities may also be accompanied by a more troubling political impulse: sovereignism. JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . Advertisement ‘No one will tell us what to do”: populist sovereignism Recent tensions with Poland over historical memory offer an illustration of this trend. The dispute concerns wartime partisan formations, some of whose members Poland accuses of committing atrocities against civilians. Statements by Ukrainian leaders, official communications, and commentary in the Ukrainian media often carried a common message: “No one will tell us who our heroes should be.” This should not be interpreted merely as an attempt to defend Ukraine’s historical narrative or seek compromise. The sentiment is understandable. For centuries Ukraine had little opportunity to tell its own story in its own voice. The current war is also a struggle for independence from Russia’s narrative about Ukraine. At the same time, virtually every EU member state – and every country aspiring to join the Union – has revised its historical memory and reshaped its national pantheon at various stages of its democratic development. Regardless of the complexities of the dispute itself, many in Poland perceive it as evidence of rising Ukrainian nationalism. The war has undoubtedly strengthened nationalist sentiment compared with the pre-2022 period, when nationalist parties remained politically marginal and failed to enter parliament. Yet what we are observing may not primarily be nationalism. A more accurate description could be sovereignism. Advertisement The dispute with Poland also generated claims that Warsaw fears Ukraine as a future economic competitor. A strong ally is welcome – but perhaps not one that becomes too strong. While certain industries may indeed face increased competition, these arguments were driven more by emotion than serious analysis. Competition is a normal feature of both the European single market and bilateral economic relations, managed through negotiation and regulation. There are other examples. In July, Kyrylo Budanov referred to Ukrainians as a “chosen nation.” Like the previous examples, this can be interpreted in different ways. Emotions were also fueled by the now-infamous Oval Office confrontation between Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, US President Donald Trump, and Vice President JD Vance in February 2025, when Zelensky was told that Ukraine “had no cards.” Eighteen months later, Ukraine appears to hold a much stronger hand. Its growing ability to strike military targets deep inside Russia with domestically developed weapons naturally strengthens national pride and confidence. It also reinforces a sense of independence from foreign partners – an important source of sovereignist thinking. Advertisement Walking through Kyiv today, one can occasionally encounter billboards urging Ukraine not to join the European Union, carrying slogans such as “Independence from Moscow – and from Brussels” or “Friendship with the EU, yes – membership, no.” The campaign is led by Ihor Shevchenko, a politician with virtually no public support. Yet its very existence may be seen as an attempt to test public sentiment regarding growing disappointment with the West. The same pattern can be observed in reactions to Russian missiles and drones violating NATO airspace. Many commentators portray both NATO and the EU as ineffective and incapable of action. This creates an obvious contradiction: if these organizations are supposedly irrelevant, why do many of the same voices still argue that Ukraine should join them? Each of these examples may seem harmless when viewed in isolation and within its specific context. Taken together, however, they suggest the emergence of a broader political trend. The only question is how influential it may become. Advertisement Why it matters As an instrument of identity politics, sovereignism is highly attractive to populists and vested interests. It offers a convenient way to divert attention from difficult reforms, obscure real governance problems behind symbolic identity conflicts, and rally public support around the flag. From a populist perspective, it is far easier to argue that “they don’t want us” than to undertake politically costly reforms required for EU accession. At times, Ukraine’s political approach toward its allies also appears dominated by an “not one step back” mentality during disputes. Once again, this may be effective identity politics. The situation looks very different, however, when hard interests are involved. A clear example came in the summer of 2025, when President Zelensky attempted to reduce the independence of Ukraine’s anti-corruption institutions. Following mass public protests and pressure from the European Union, the proposal was ultimately withdrawn. Ukraine continues to enjoy broad Western support – particularly from NATO’s eastern flank and the Nordic countries – despite periodic political disagreements. That support is unlikely to disappear, nor should it. However, the quality of these partnerships will increasingly depend on Ukraine’s own policies, including domestic governance. There is nothing wrong with national pride or self-confidence, especially for a country fighting for its survival. But building politics around these emotions alone rarely leads to good outcomes. Sovereignism may appear attractive, yet in practice it risks sliding into provincialism. Signs of sovereignist thinking can be found across the Ukrainian political spectrum, although fortunately it remains far from dominant. Recent mass demonstrations against the dismissal of Mykhailo Fedorov – widely seen as the face of Ukraine’s reform agenda – suggest that many Ukrainians still prioritize modernization over populism. Advertisement That is precisely what Ukraine needs: to stay firmly on its pro-Western course, pursue pragmatism and choose reformers over populists. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: 1:44 Australia to impose 'targeted measures' to stop Israeli settler violence but no import ban – video Australian politics Australia considers new Israel sanctions but won’t join UK in banning trade with ‘settler terrorists’ Penny Wong has concerns about blanket ban announced by UK, France and Canada, but says new ‘targeted measures’ planned over Israeli settlers Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Tom McIlroy Political editor Tue 8 Sep 2026 21.38 EDT Last modified on Tue 8 Sep 2026 22.06 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Australia is preparing another round of sanctions against Israel but has stopped short of joining the UK in banning trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank . Overnight, the UK government offered its strongest condemnation yet of Israel’s occupation , with the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, calling efforts to control the West Bank unlawful. He said his government agreed there was “ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in areas of the West Bank, perpetrated by settler terrorists”. The UK will ban goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories, and introduce a new ban on arms licences and other exports. Sanctions against individuals are also planned. Australia considers new Israel sanctions but won’t join UK in banning trade with ‘settler terrorists’ Read more In a joint statement, the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, the French president, Emmanuel Macron, and Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, said they were taking further action to push for progress on a two-state solution. Nine European countries have also said they were considering similar measures. While Australia has previously acted in concert with partners overseas, the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, said Australia was not currently pushing for a broad ban on goods produced in Israeli settlements. “Australia is pursuing further targeted measures in coordination with international partners to deter illegal settlements and settler violence,” Wong said. “We have concerns about the implementation of a blanket ban and unintended consequences for Australian businesses, for Palestinians and for Israelis, and we will continue to work with partners to protect the prospects of a two-state solution.” Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email But Wong said the Israeli government was “extinguishing the possibility of a two-state solution” through violence and expansion of settlements in the West Bank. Wong called on Israeli government to stop violence between settlers and Palestinians, including the destruction of property, displacement of families, torture, sexual assault and killings. The foreign affairs ministers of 12 countries have also released a statement regarding possible sanctions over the settlements. “Today, Canada, Denmark, Finland, France, Iceland, Ireland, Norway, ⁠Poland, Portugal, Spain, ⁠Sweden and the UK confirm their intention to introduce national and or support ⁠European restrictions on trade in goods ⁠with settlements which ⁠are illegal under international law, or that they are actively considering these and ‌other measures, in accordance with their national procedures,” the joint statement said. It comes amid tense relations between Australia and the Netanyahu government after the 7 October terror attacks by Hamas, the subsequent Israel-Gaza war, and the Bondi Beach terror attack in December. Australia has instituted financial sanctions and tough travel bans on some Israelis in response to violence in the West Bank. Sanctions are also in place against two members of Netanyahu’s government, Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich. Wong has been working with the family of the killed Australian aid worker Zomi Frankcom on a response to the Israel Defense Forces’ decision not to open a criminal investigation into Gaza strikes that killed her and six of her colleagues. Ed Husic, the Labor backbencher who has pushed the government to take further action, said the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, believed his government could “ride out” statements from countries that criticise it. Zomi Frankcom did not deserve to die. Israel’s refusal to investigate her death and its failure to apologise is despicable | Geoffrey Robertson Read more “It cannot ride out the impact of sanctions,” he said on Tuesday. “This is a big seismic move. “Australia is going to need to do the same because we can’t say we’re for the state of Palestine , which I am very much a supporter of, and ignore the fact that illegal settlements are undermining the ability for a state of Palestine to emerge. We need to take action.” Asked about Britain’s moves, Coalition frontbencher Julian Leeser said he was critical of the Albanese government’s foreign policy towards Israel. “They’re always looking for opportunities to have a go at our democratic ally in the Middle East,” he said. “I think that our foreign policy should be based on two principles: we should stand for our values, and we should stand with our friends.” The Australia/Israel and Jewish Affairs Council’s executive director, Colin Rubenstein, rejected suggestions Israel and the settlements were preventing peace, instead blaming the Palestinian Authority. “Sanctioning Israel will only be counterproductive, in encouraging further Palestinian intransigence, and will further draw Australia away from our traditional bipartisan and beneficial relationship with Israel,” he said. “If we are serious about pursuing principled foreign policy and encouraging peace, rather than catering to domestic political considerations and appeasing extremist factions, we will withdraw our recognition of the Palestinian state and sanction the PA, not Israel.” New Zealand’s foreign affairs minister, Winston Peters, said he was “deeply concerned” by the deteriorating situation in the West Bank and the escalation in Israel’s actions jeopardised the prospect of “durable peace”. He stopped short of joining the UK in placing a ban on trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank, saying New Zealand has not traditionally pursued trade measures to address foreign policy issues. https://www.politico.eu/article/deutschl.text: BRÜSSEL - Deutschland und Spanien heizen den Streit darüber an, wie die Made-in-Europe-Regeln im Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA) ausgelegt werden sollen. Beide Regierungen lancierten ihre gegensätzlichen Standpunkte über inoffizielle Diskussionspapiere (Non Paper) in Brüssel. Sie stellten damit die Weichen für harte Verhandlungen über das EU-Gesetz zur Industriepolitik. Die Europäische Kommission hat den IAA im März vorgestellt . Er sieht unter anderem vor, staatliche Aufträge und Förderprogramme der EU-Länder für grüne Technologien, energieintensive Industrie und die Automobilbranche stärker auf Unternehmen aus der EU zu lenken. Dies soll ihnen im Wettbewerb mit Exporteuren aus China helfen. Sechs Monate später ringen die 27 Regierungen der Union immer noch um eine gemeinsame Basis. Umstritten ist vor allem die Frage, ob Made-in-Europa-Privilegien nur für Firmen aus der EU, aus dem gesamten Europa oder auch für Länder gelten soll, die EU-Firmen ihrerseits Zugang zu öffentlichen Aufträgen gewähren. Advertisement Advertisement In der EU geht es um Aufträge, die einen erheblichen Teil der Wirtschaftsleistung ausmachen. Von Windparks bis hin zu Stahl und Zement für den Bau von Autobahnen und U-Bahnen. Deutschland, das Exportkraftzentrum der Union, dringt auf eine breiter angelegte „Made with Europe“-Definition. Dies entspricht auch weitgehend dem ursprünglichen Vorschlag der Kommission. Er sieht die Aufnahme von Partnern vor, die Freihandels- oder Beschaffungsabkommen mit der EU geschlossen haben oder einer Zollunion mit der Union angehören. Der Kreis könnte bis zu 80 Länder umfassen. „Deutschland lehnt Protektionismus und Diskriminierung ab“, heißt es in dem deutschen Papier . „Die EU muss ein verlässlicher Partner für ihre Freihandelspartner bleiben und ihren rechtlichen Verpflichtungen nachkommen.“ Außerdem wird darin eine „Opt-in“-Möglichkeit gefordert, um Staaten einzubeziehen, die EU-Firmen eine entsprechende Behandlung gewähren. Dem deutschen Papier haben sich bisher keine anderen EU-Länder angeschlossen. Frankreich, die zweitgrößte Volkswirtschaft der Union, dringt wie Spanien in die entgegengesetzte Richtung und plädiert für einen restriktiveren Ansatz . Der französische Industrieminister Sébastien Martin bestritt zwar nicht, dass Europa gegenüber Handelspartnern offen bleiben müsse, betonte jedoch, dass öffentliches Geld in die Produktion in Europa fließen müsse. „Auch in Zukunft wird es möglich sein, Produkte zu haben, bei denen ein Teil der Wertschöpfung aus anderen Ländern stammt, aber die Produktion muss in Europa stattfinden, damit sie für öffentliche Fördermittel infrage kommen“, sagte Martin bei seiner Ankunft zur Sitzung am Donnerstag in Brüssel. Advertisement Advertisement Zwiebelsystem Um das Konzept europäischer Präferenzen umsetzbar zu machen, hat Spanien laut seinem Papier eine dreistufige Struktur vorgeschlagen , bei der in der EU hergestellte Produkte die höchste Präferenz erhalten würden. „Ein differenzierterer und risikobasierter Ansatz könnte sowohl die Wirksamkeit als auch die politische Akzeptanz des Textes verbessern“, heißt es in dem Dokument. Die 27 EU-Mitgliedstaaten würden die erste Stufe bilden, während die zweite Stufe die Mitglieder des Europäischen Wirtschaftsraums und andere „vertrauenswürdige“ Partner umfassen würde. Eine dritte Stufe wäre für Länder vorgesehen, die ein Freihandelsabkommen, eine Zollunion oder ein Beschaffungsabkommen mit der EU geschlossen haben. Ihr Status könnte auf die zweite Stufe angehoben werden, wenn sie ihre Handelsabkommen mit der EU vertiefen, heißt es in dem Papier. Irland, das bis Ende des Jahres den Vorsitz im EU-Rat hat, bemüht sich, die Differenzen zu überbrücken. Dublin wird am 7. Oktober eine Sitzung der stellvertretenden Botschafter einberufen und plant, bis Mitte des Monats einen neuen Kompromissvorschlag vorzulegen, teilte Industrieminister Peter Burke seinen Kollegen am Donnerstag mit. Man hofft, im November eine Einigung zu erzielen. Die Meinungsverschiedenheiten zwischen den EU-Regierungen ziehen sich auch durch die Parteien: Der deutsche und der spanische Flügel der Europäischen Volkspartei – der größten Fraktion im Europäischen Parlament – sind beim Industriegesetz ähnlich gespalten . Advertisement Advertisement Die federführenden Abgeordneten des EU-Parlaments werden ihren Berichtsentwurf voraussichtlich am 28. September erörtern, während die Abgeordneten bis zum 7. Oktober Änderungsanträge einreichen können. Die Frist wurde auf Antrag der EVP um eine Woche verlängert. Erst wenn Rat und Parlament ihre Standpunkte festgelegt haben, können Verhandlungen zwischen den EU-Institutionen aufgenommen werden. Das Ziel der Kommission, noch in diesem Jahr eine Einigung zu erzielen, erscheint zunehmend unrealistisch. Die Debatte darüber, wer in den Club aufgenommen wird, wird in Großbritannien besonders aufmerksam verfolgt. Der langwierige Gesetzgebungsprozess der EU erschwert die Bemühungen des Vereinigten Königreichs, seine Beziehungen zu Brüssel neu zu gestalten. Die Regierung des neuen Premierministers Andy Burnham hat ihre Bedenken hinsichtlich eines Ausschlusses von „Made in Europe“ in die Diskussion eingebracht . EU-Vertreter haben darauf geantwortet, dass sie das Ergebnis des Gesetzgebungsverfahrens zum „Industrial Accelerator Act“ nicht vorwegnehmen können.
